The Escalation Service Function →

Modeling Escalation State

A new slaBreachedAt column on Ticket — the first schema change since Week 2 — and why the scan needs it to avoid re-escalating the same ticket forever.

"Scan open tickets past a threshold and escalate" (PLAN.md) sounds like a read-only query, but running it on repeat immediately raises a question: once a ticket has been escalated, the next scan will still find it — it's still open, still past the threshold — so it would escalate again, and again, every time the job runs. Something has to record "already escalated" so the scan can skip it next time.

That something is a new column on Ticket:

// Figure 6.2: escalation state on Ticket (prisma/schema.prisma)
model Ticket {
  // ...existing columns from Week 2...
  slaBreachedAt DateTime?
}

null means "not yet breached"; a timestamp means "breached, and here's when." This is deliberately its own column rather than a new TicketStatus value (open / in_progress / resolved / closed, unchanged since Week 2) — SLA breach is a fact layered on top of the customer-facing workflow status, not a replacement for it. A ticket can be open and breached at the same time; folding "breached" into status would mean a ticket can no longer be both, and would force every existing status-based query in ticket.service.js to account for a state that has nothing to do with what the customer sees.

This is the first schema change since the Week 2 migration — a reminder that "the data model is settled" was never a permanent claim, just true until a new requirement (here, idempotent escalation) needs a place to live that nothing existing covers.
